Whether it be verbal expression or provocation—
foreseeing this danger in the future,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Thus, with a companion, may I be"—this means he has craving as his companion, or a person as his companion.
How does he have craving as his companion?
"Craving" refers to craving for forms … [as above] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
He in whom this craving is not abandoned is called "one who has craving as his companion.
A person with craving as his companion wanders for a long time through the cycle of existence.
"From this state to another state,
one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Thus, one has craving as one's companion.

How does one have a person as a companion? Here, someone who is agitated and of unpeaceful mind, neither for the sake of a purpose nor for the sake of a reason, becomes a companion to one, or a third to two, or a fourth to three.
Therein, he prattles much idle chatter.
Namely: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks,
talk of clothing, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of scents, talk of relatives, and talk of vehicles.
He speaks about villages, towns, cities, and countries; he speaks about women, heroes, streets, and wells;
he speaks about departed relatives, various kinds of talk, speculations about the world, speculations about the ocean, and talk concerning "thus it was" and "thus it will be.
Thus he has a person as his companion.
Thus there would be association with a second person.
"Vocal expression and provocation" means that "vocal expression" refers to the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*), namely:
talk about kings... [and so forth].
Such is the talk of existence and non-existence.
"Or provocation" means there are two kinds of provocation:
provocation by craving and provocation by views... [etc. ...
"This is an attachment through craving" ...
[and so on] ... "this is an attachment through views"—this verbal expression is "assailing."
"Perceiving this danger in the future": "danger" means the danger of birth,
the danger of aging, the danger of illness, the danger of death, the danger of kings, the danger of thieves, the danger of fire, the danger of water,
the danger of self-reproach, the danger of reproach by others, the danger of punishment, the danger of an evil rebirth, and the danger of waves.

The fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, the fear of sharks, the fear for one’s livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of timidity in assemblies, the fear of intoxication—the terror, the trepidation, the horripilation, the agitation of the mind, and the dread.
"Foreseeing this fear in the future" means: foreseeing this fear in the future, seeing it, looking at it, contemplating it, and examining it.
Foreseeing this danger in the future, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore that Paccekasambuddha said:
“Thus there would be a companion for me.”
Or verbal expression, or even hostility;
seeing this danger in the future,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and enchanting;
they agitate the mind with their diverse forms.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure,
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and enchanting.
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmā): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures.
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.

"Variegated" means of various colors: forms of various colors, sounds of various colors, odors of various colors, tastes of various colors, and tangibles of various colors—desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
"Sweet" is what was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure."
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on].
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Whatever happiness and gladness arise dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure, a filthy pleasure, a vulgar pleasure, an ignoble pleasure; it is not to be cultivated, nor...
"It should be developed but not cultivated; one should fear this pleasure," so I say—
for sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet,
and delightful.
That which is the mind (*manas*) … [as above] … that is the corresponding mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
They delight, praise, gladden, and exhilarate the mind;
thus, sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are indeed variegated, sweet, and charming.
"With forms of various shapes they agitate the mind" means: with forms of many colors ...
[and so on] ... with tangibles of many colors they agitate, please, and delight the mind;
thus, "with forms of various shapes they agitate the mind."
"Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures?"
In this case, monks, a clansman earns his livelihood by means of a craft—
whether by calculation, accounting, reckoning, agriculture, trade,
cattle-herding, archery, service to the king, or any other craft— facing cold, facing heat, and facing the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles.
Being touched by contact, he dies tormented by hunger and thirst.

Monks, this is the visible danger in sensual pleasures: this mass of suffering, with sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, and having sensual pleasures alone as its cause.

If, monks, those possessions do not come to fruition for that clansman despite his rising up, striving, and exerting himself, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
“Alas, my exertion was in vain! Alas, my effort was fruitless!

Monks, this too is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

And if, monks, those riches do not come to fruition for that clansman despite his thus exerting himself, striving, and making an effort, he experiences pain and grief on account of the protection of those riches.
‘How can it be that kings do not seize my wealth, nor thieves steal it, nor fire burn it, nor water carry it away, nor unloved heirs take it?
Yet, despite guarding and protecting it in this way, those very riches are seized by kings or stolen by thieves, or burnt by fire, or carried away by water, or taken by unloved heirs.
He grieves... [and so on].
One falls into confusion, thinking: "Even that which I had no longer exists.

Monks, this too is a visible danger regarding sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as the cause, sensual pleasures as the source, and sensual pleasures as the basis— precisely because of sensual pleasures—
kings quarrel with kings, kshatriyas quarrel with kshatriyas, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders;
even a mother quarrels with her son, and a son quarrels with his mother.
The father quarrels with the son, the son quarrels with the father; the brother quarrels with the sister, the sister quarrels with the brother;
the companion quarrels with the companion.
Having fallen into such strife, contention, and dispute, they attack one another with their hands, they attack with clods of earth, they attack with sticks, and they attack with weapons.
There they meet even death, or suffering equal to death.

This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger regarding sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering with sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and with sensual pleasure itself as its cause.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and with sensual pleasure itself as its cause, [they take up] sword and shield...
Taking up their bows and quivers and donning their armor, they charge into a battle arrayed on both sides—
amidst arrows being shot, spears being hurled, and swords flashing. There,
they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, and have their heads cut off by swords.
There they meet with death or suffering amounting to death.

This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger regarding sensual pleasures—a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as their very cause, [beings take up] sword and shield...
Taking up their bows and quivers and donning their armor, they charge into the fray— while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled,
and swords are flashing. There, they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears,
drenched with boiling cow-dung, crushed under heavy mallets, and have their heads severed with swords.
There they undergo even death, or suffering equal to death.

This too, monks, is a visible danger regarding sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

Furthermore, monks, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as their very cause, one may even enter into a secret alliance...
They cut [the crops], they steal even what is hidden, they commit burglary, they lie in ambush on the road, and they go to another’s wife.
Kings seize them and subject them to various punishments:
they flog them with whips, they flog them with canes, they flog them with split rods; they cut off their hands... [and so on] ...they cut off their heads with a sword.
There they undergo even death, or suffering equal to death.

This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger regarding sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering with sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and sensual pleasure itself as its root.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasure as cause, sensual pleasure as source, sensual pleasure as basis, and sensual pleasure itself as root, they engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

"Having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

This too, bhikkhus, is a danger regarding sensual pleasures—a mass of suffering in the future, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
"Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure": this means having seen, perceived, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore that Paccekasambuddha said:
“Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet, and delightful...”
They churn the mind with hideous forms;
having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This plague, this tumor, this calamity, this disease, this arrow,
and this fear— having seen this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, [one should abandon them].
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Calamity, tumor, affliction, disease, dart, and fear—these are the designations for sensual pleasures, O monks. It was further said:
"Fear, O monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures."
“Suffering,” monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
“Disease,” monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
“Abscess,” monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
“Arrows,” monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
“Entanglements,” monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
“Mud,” monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
"Bhikkhus, 'the womb' is a designation for sensual pleasures.
And why, bhikkhus, are they called 'fearsome'?

Because one who is stained by lust for sensual pleasures, bound by desire and lust, is not released from fears pertaining to the present life, nor is he released from fears pertaining to future lives; therefore, 'fearsome' is a designation for sensual pleasures."
And why, monks, is it suffering? … [and so on] … a disease?
… a tumor? … [and so on].
A dart...
a snare...
a mire...
“‘Womb’ is a designation for sensual pleasures.

Because one who is stained by lust for sensual pleasures, monks, and bound by desire and lust, is not released from wombs pertaining to this present life, nor is he released from wombs pertaining to future lives; therefore, ‘womb’ is a designation for sensual pleasures.
Fear, suffering, and disease—
The boil, the arrow, and the attachment;
the mire and the womb— both of these are called sensual pleasures.
Wherein the ordinary person,
a being submerged by the appearance of pleasure,
goes again to the womb.
But when a bhikkhu is ardent,
he does not lack clear comprehension.
He [crosses] this quagmire, this difficult path;
Having transcended such a state,
he gazes upon the writhing multitude beset by birth and old age.
“Plague, tumor, calamity, disease, dart, and danger— this is what they are.
Having seen this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, having seen it, weighed it, scrutinized it, analyzed it, and made it manifest— this is the meaning.
Seeing this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus said that Paccekasambuddha: “Disease, swelling, and calamity,”
This is disease, this is a dart,
this is fear; seeing this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having fully endured cold and heat, hunger and thirst,
wind and sun, and gadflies and snakes;
all these indeed having overcome,
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
"Cold" is cold for two reasons: [namely,] by way of external temperature and by way of internal sensation.
It is cold either due to an internal disturbance of the elements or due to external climatic conditions.
It is hot for two reasons—
it is hot either due to an internal disturbance of the elements or due to external climatic conditions.
"Hunger" is said to be hunger;
"thirst" is said to be thirst for water—thus:
cold and heat, hunger and thirst.
"Regarding wind and heat, and gadflies and serpents":
"Wind" refers to east winds, west winds, north winds, south winds; winds with dust, winds without dust;
cold winds, hot winds; slight winds, intense winds, and *verambha* winds, wing-winds, and garuḷa-winds.
"Palmyra-leaf fans" refers to the wind from fanning;
"sun" refers to the heat of the sun;
"gadflies" refers to brown flies.
"Reptiles" means snakes— that is, wind, heat, gadflies, and reptiles.
"Having overcome all these" means having mastered them, having overwhelmed them, having exhausted them, and having crushed them.
Having fully mastered all these, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus that Paccekasambuddha said:
“Cold and heat, hunger and thirst...”
Wind and heat, gadflies and serpents—
having overcome all these,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like a bull elephant who has left the herds behind,
with his shoulders grown and magnificent as a lotus,
may you dwell in the forest as you please.
"One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Like an elephant avoiding herds"—here "elephant" (nāga) refers to a great bull elephant; the paccekabuddha is also called an "elephant."
For what reason is a Paccekasambuddha called a *nāga*?
He is called a *nāga* because he does not commit sin (*āgu*);
he is called a *nāga* because he does not go [astray].
He does not come (āgacchati), thus he is a *nāga*.
How is that Paccekasambuddha a *nāga* because he does not commit offenses (*āgu*)?

"Offense" (*āgu*) refers to evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death.
He does nothing at all in the world,
having cast off all fetters and bonds;
liberated, he clings to nothing anywhere.
A *nāga* is called such because of being "thus" (*tathattā*).
Thus, that Paccekasambuddha is a *nāga* because he does not commit any transgression (*āguṃ na karoti*).
How is it that this Paccekasambuddha is a *nāga* because he does not go?
Thus, the Paccekabuddha does not fall into a course of action through desire,
he does not fall into a course of action through hatred,
and he does not fall into a course of action through delusion.
He does not go by way of fear,
he does not go under the influence of lust,
and he does not go under the influence of hatred.
He does not proceed under the influence of delusion,
he does not proceed under the influence of conceit,
and he does not proceed under the influence of views.
He does not proceed by way of restlessness,
he does not proceed by way of doubt,
and he does not proceed by way of underlying tendencies.
He is not carried away, led, swept along, or dragged by worldly phenomena.
Thus, that paccekasambuddha is a *nāga* because he does not go.
How is it that this paccekasambuddha is a *nāga* because he does not come?
By means of the path of stream-entry, those defilements which have been abandoned are not repeated, are not returned to,
and are not revisited; by means of the path of once-returning …pe… by means of the path of non-returning …pe…
Those defilements which have been abandoned by means of the path of arahantship, he does not bring back, does not return to, and does not go back toward them.
Thus, that Paccekabuddha does not come [back] and is therefore a *nāga*.
"Like an elephant avoiding the herds" means just as that elephant-nāga, having avoided and shunned the herds...
Having avoided [the company of others], he wanders, dwells, conducts himself, behaves, protects, maintains, and sustains himself all alone,
having plunged into the midst of the forest wilderness. A Paccekasambuddha, too, having avoided, shunned,
and eschewed the crowd, resorts to remote lodgings in the forest depths— solitary places, free from noise, free from clamor, and secluded from the presence of people.
These are the secrets of men, suitable for solitude.
He goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone;
he enters the village alone for alms, returns alone, sits alone in private, undertakes walking meditation alone, and wanders, dwells, and conducts himself alone.
"He causes them to turn, protects them, maintains them,
and supports them"— just as an elephant, having avoided the herds;
"with trunk grown, lotus-like, and magnificent," just as that elephant-nāga has a fully developed trunk measuring seven cubits.
He is eighteen cubits tall; and a Paccekasambuddha likewise has fully developed the aggregates:

the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.

Just as that noble elephant is "lotus-like," so too the Paccekasambuddha is "lotus-like" by means of the seven flowers of the factors of enlightenment: the flower of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment,
the flower of the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment, the flower of the energy factor of enlightenment, the flower of the rapture factor of enlightenment,
the flower of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, and the flower of the concentration factor of enlightenment.
By means of the flower of the equanimity factor of enlightenment.

Just as that noble elephant is preeminent in stature, strength, speed, and courage, so too the Paccekabuddha is preeminent in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—
he is the "Lotus-Bearer" with his trunk fully grown and is preeminent.
"Live in the forest as you please": just as that elephant-king lives in the forest as he pleases, so too does the Paccekasambuddha live in the forest as he pleases.
He lives in the forest as he pleases with the first jhāna, and with the second jhāna... [and so on].
With the third jhāna...
with the fourth jhāna as well, he dwells in the forest as long as he wishes;
with the liberation of mind through loving-kindness as well, he dwells in the forest as long as he wishes.

He dwells in the forest for as long as he desires, [cultivating] the liberation of mind through compassion, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy, and the liberation of mind through equanimity.
He dwells in the forest for as long as he wishes, having attained the sphere of infinite space;
likewise, having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness;
and likewise, having attained the sphere of nothingness.

He dwells in the forest for as long as he wishes— even in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even in the attainment of cessation, and even in the attainment of fruition.
Dwell as you please in the forest; wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus that Paccekabuddha said:
“Like an elephant, having avoided the herds...”
With shoulders well-rounded, lotus-eyed, and noble—
dwell as you please in the forest;
wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience temporary liberation,
even if they were to heed the words of the Kinsman of the Sun.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who delights in company, there is no occasion for that temporary liberation which he might otherwise encounter; thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"To whatever extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu delights in company, takes pleasure in company, is devoted to delighting in company, and delights in the crowd..."
"One who delights in the crowd, rejoices in the crowd, and is devoted to the pleasure of the crowd—

it is impossible that he will obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, that happiness which is the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of enlightenment."
But as for that bhikkhu, Ānanda, who dwells alone, withdrawn from the crowd— it is to be expected of that bhikkhu that he will obtain at will,

without difficulty, and without hardship, that happiness which is the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of enlightenment; this is possible.
To whatever extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who delights in company, takes pleasure in company, is devoted to delighting in company; who delights in a group,
takes pleasure in a group, rejoices in a group, and is devoted to delighting in a group— will he enter and dwell in a pleasant temporary liberation of mind,
or will he enter and dwell in the unshakable liberation that is not temporary?— [he will not.]
This is not possible. But for that bhikkhu, Ānanda, who dwells alone, withdrawn from the crowd,
it is to be expected that he will attain and dwell in either a temporary, pleasant liberation of mind, or one that is non-temporary.
"Or they do not waver; it is possible that this may happen"—this refers to the impossibility for one who delights in company to experience temporary liberation.
"Reflecting on the words of the Kinsman of the Sun": the sun is called *āditya*.
Thus Gotama by clan;
the Paccekasambuddha also is Gotama by clan.
That Paccekasambuddha is a kinsman and relative by clan to the Sun; therefore the Paccekasambuddha is the Kinsman of the Ādicca (Solar) lineage.

"Having heeded the word of the Kinsman of the Sun": having heard, listened to, mastered, retained, and discerned the word, the manner of speech, the teaching, and the instruction of the Kinsman of the Sun—thus, "having heeded the word of the Kinsman of the Sun," one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Thus spoke that Paccekasambuddha.
“It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience temporary liberation,
even if they were to heed the words of the Kinsman of the Sun.”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The second chapter.
3. The third chapter.
Having transcended the thicket of views,
having reached the certainty of rightness and attained the path,
I have arisen with knowledge and am no longer led by others.
"One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, having transcended the thorny brambles of views.
By "thorny brambles of views" is meant the twenty-based view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
Here, the uninstructed worldling is one who has not seen the Noble Ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones.

One who does not see true persons, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form;
[and likewise] feeling ... [and so on].

One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as being in self, or self as being in perception. One regards volitional formations as self... One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
Whatever view such as this is—a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views;

a seizing, a grasping, an adherence, a misapprehension; a wrong path, a false road, falsity, a sectarian stand, a perverted seizing, a distorted seizing, a reversal of seizing, a wrong seizing—regarding what is not as it truly is.
"According to how it is" is the grasping; as far as the sixty-two types of speculative views—these are the "tangles of views.
"One who has transcended the tangles of views" means one who has gone beyond, passed over, surmounted, and transcended the tangles of views.
He has transcended the diversities of views.

Having reached the certainty and attained the path, "certainty" refers to the four paths; namely, the noble eightfold path, which is as follows: [the right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration].
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
One who is endowed with the four noble paths— one who has entered the certainty, reached it, attained it, touched it, and realized it— is said to have "attained the certainty."

"One who has attained the path" means one who has gained the path, attained the path, reached the path, touched the path, and realized the path—one who has entered the fixed course of rightness and attained the path.
"I have arisen knowledge and am no longer led by others": the knowledge of that Paccekasambuddha has arisen, fully arisen, been produced, fully produced, and become manifest.
The knowledge that “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent” has arisen, fully arisen, been produced, been brought forth, and become manifest;
[the knowledge] that “all conditioned phenomena are suffering” …pe… [and] that “all phenomena are non-self” …pe….
“The knowledge that ‘whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation’ has arisen, fully arisen, been produced, fully produced, and become manifest—thus I am one whose knowledge has arisen.
He is ‘not to be led by others’;

that Paccekasambuddha is not led by another, does not rely on another, does not depend on another, and is not bound to another; he knows and sees according to reality, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful.”

“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’— not led by others, not dependent on others, not subject to others, not bound to others— he knows and sees it as it truly is, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful.
‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’ …pe… ‘All phenomena are non-self’ …pe…”

“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation”—knowing and seeing this thus as it really is, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful, one is not led by others, does not depend on others, is not reliant on others, and is not bound to others;
I have arisen knowledge such that I am not to be led by another. Let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore that Paccekabuddha said:
“Having transcended the thorns of views,
I have reached the certainty, having attained the path.”
“I have attained knowledge and am no longer led by others;
let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Free from greed, free from deceit, and free from thirst,
Free from hypocrisy, with delusion and impurities burnt away,
and having become desireless toward the entire world,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Free from greed, free from deceit, free from thirst"—here "greed" refers to craving.
That which is lust, infatuation... [as above] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—that greed, that craving, has been abandoned by that Paccekasambuddha;
it has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Paccekasambuddha is free from greed.
He is "one who is devoid of guile" (nikkuho); there are three bases for guile:
the basis of guile consisting in the seeking of requisites, the basis of guile consisting in deportment, and the basis of guile consisting in indirect hinting.
What is the ground for hypocrisy known as the acceptance of requisites?
Here, householders invite a bhikkhu with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
he, being of evil desire and overcome by longing, is desirous of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Out of a desire for more, he renounces robes, renounces almsfood, renounces lodgings,
and renounces medicinal requisites for the sick.
He speaks thus:
“What is the use of an expensive robe for a recluse?
It is fitting that a recluse should gather rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shopkeeper’s discarded cloth, and having made them into a patched cloak, wear it.
What is the use of expensive almsfood for a recluse?”
It is fitting that a recluse should maintain his life by means of alms-food gathered from door to door;
what need has a recluse for a costly dwelling?
It is fitting that a recluse should be a dweller at the foot of a tree, or a dweller in a charnel ground, or a dweller in the open air.
"What need has a recluse for costly medicinal requisites for the sick?
It is fitting that a recluse should prepare medicine with putrid urine or pieces of gall-nut.
From that time forth, he wore coarse robes, ate coarse almsfood, used a coarse resting place, and used coarse medicinal requisites for the sick.
The householders know of him thus:
"This ascetic is of few desires, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, and a proponent of the ascetic practices.
Consequently, they increasingly invite him with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Thus he spoke:
“Through the presence of three things, a faithful clansman generates much merit; through the presence of faith, a faithful clansman generates much merit;
through the presence of the gift to be given, a faithful clansman [generates much merit].”
One generates much merit; through the presence of those worthy of offerings, a faithful clansman generates much merit.
You have this faith, the gift to be given exists, and I am the recipient.
If I do not accept it, you will thus be excluded from merit.
"I have no need for this;
however, out of compassion for you alone, I accept it.
From that time on, he accepts much robe-cloth, accepts much almsfood, accepts much lodging, and accepts much medicinal requisites for the sick.
Such frowning, frowardness, scheming, scheming behavior, and a scheming state of mind—
this is the ground for scheming known as the seeking of requisites.
What is the ground for scheming known as deportment?
In this case, someone with evil desires, driven by longing and intent on gaining esteem— thinking,
"In this way people will hold me in high regard"— regulates his walking, regulates his standing, regulates his sitting, and regulates his reclining; he walks with deliberate intent,
stands with deliberate intent, sits with deliberate intent, and lies down with deliberate intent, as if concentrated.
He walks as if composed, stands as if composed, sits as if composed, and lies down as if composed; he is like one who meditates on the threshold.
Whatever such posing, setting, adjusting, grimacing, grimacery, hypocrisy, scheming, and scheming-ness there is in regard to deportment—this is [hypocrisy].
This is the ground for hypocrisy consisting in deportment.
What is the ground for hypocrisy consisting in indirect hinting?
Here, a certain person of evil desires, driven by desire and intent on gaining esteem, speaks words based on the noble Dhamma with the thought, "In this way, people will hold me in high esteem."
“He who wears such a robe is a monk of great influence,” he says;
“he who wears such a bowl … [and so on] … he who wears a bronze dish …”
He carries a needle-case;
he carries a water-strainer;
he carries a key.
"He wears sandals...
he wears a waistband...
he wears a shoulder-strap; that ascetic is one of great influence," he says.
“He whose preceptor is such as this, that ascetic is of great influence,” he says; “he whose teacher is such as this … [and so on] … he whose co-preceptors are such as these …”
... fellow students ...
friends ...
those seen in person ...
“He is one who shares his meals… he is a companion; that ascetic is of great influence,” he says;
“he who dwells in such a dwelling…”
He dwells in a wealthy carriage,
he dwells in a palace,
he dwells on a terrace.
He dwells in a cave… he dwells in a grotto… he dwells in a hut…
He dwells in a gabled house;
he dwells in a watchtower;
he dwells in a multi-storied building.
He dwells in the open air;
he dwells in the assembly hall;
he dwells in a pavilion.
“He is a recluse of great power who dwells at the foot of a tree,” he says.
Or else, being full of hypocrisy, full of frowning looks, full of deceit, full of chatter, and seeking honor through his mouth, he speaks of such profound [states]:
“This recluse is an attainer of such peaceful dwellings and meditative attainments. Thus he speaks of that which is deep...
He speaks words that are hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane, and connected with emptiness.
Such grimacing, grimacery, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of being a schemer—this is the basis for scheming known as "hinting.
For that Paccekasambuddha, these three bases for scheming have been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
Therefore, that Paccekasambuddha is free from deceit.
"Free from thirst" (*nippipāsa*): "thirst" (*pipāsā*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness.
That thirst, that craving, has been abandoned by that paccekabuddha, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the paccekabuddha is "free from thirst"—
meaning he is free from greed, free from deceit, and free from thirst.
"Free from hypocrisy, with taints and delusion burnt away.
Here, "hypocrisy" (*makkha*) refers to that which is hypocrisy, the act of being hypocritical, the state of being hypocritical, harshness, and the performance of harsh deeds.
"Taints" (*kasāva*) refers to lust as a taint, hatred as a taint, and delusion as a taint; anger... resentment... hypocrisy... spite—all unwholesome volitional formations are taints.

There is ignorance regarding suffering, ignorance regarding the origin of suffering, ignorance regarding the cessation of suffering, and ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
there is ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, ignorance regarding both the past and the future,
and ignorance regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.
Whatever such lack of knowledge, non-seeing, non-realization, non-awakening, non-penetration,
non-comprehension, non-mastery, non-exploration, non-regard, non-reviewing, lack of direct experience, dullness, folly, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, confusion,

total bewilderment, ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the snare of ignorance, and the root of unwholesomeness that is delusion— this is so.

The hypocrisy, the impurity, and the delusion of that Paccekasambuddha have been vomited up, cast out, blown away, abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, and calmed; they are incapable of arising again, burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
That Paccekasambuddha is free from hypocrisy, having blown away impurity and delusion.
Having become one who has no longing for the entire world—"longing" here refers to craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, and root of unwholesomeness there is.

"In all the world" means: in the entire world of the woeful states, the entire world of humans, the entire world of devas, the entire world of aggregates, the entire world of elements, and the entire world of sense bases.
"Having become one who has no longing for all the world" means: having become one who has no longing for all the world, having become free from craving, having become free from thirst.
Having become free from longing for the entire world, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore, that Paccekasambuddha said:
“Free from greed, free from deceit, free from thirst...”
Free from hypocrisy, with delusion and impurities burnt away,
having become one who has no longing for the entire world,
let him wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One should avoid an evil companion who sees no harm and is intent on what is wrong;
one should not associate with one who is addicted to vice or is heedless.
"One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros;
one should avoid an evil companion.
By "evil companion" is meant a companion who is possessed of the tenfold wrong view.
There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; and there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge.
"Having realized the world for themselves through direct higher knowledge, they proclaim it"—
this is one who has evil companions.
One should avoid an evil companion.
"One should avoid a bad companion; one should shun a bad companion"—one should indeed shun a bad companion.
"One who sees no harm and is settled in the uneven"—one who sees no harm is said to be a companion possessed of the tenfold wrong view.
"There is no gift, there is no sacrifice... [and so on] ...those who, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known.
They are established in what is uneven: established in uneven bodily action, established in uneven verbal action, established in uneven mental action;
established in uneven killing of living beings, established in uneven taking of what is not given, established in uneven [actions].
Established in sexual misconduct; established in false speech that is uneven; established in divisive speech that is uneven;
established in harsh speech that is uneven; established in idle chatter that is uneven; established in covetousness that is uneven;
established in ill will that is uneven; established in wrong view that is uneven; [established] in things that are uneven...
Settled in volitional formations, settled in the five uneven strands of sensual pleasure, settled and deeply settled in the five uneven hindrances,
attached, clung to, approached, obsessed with, and intent upon them—
one who sees no benefit and is settled in what is uneven.
"One should not associate with one who is addicted or heedless.

Here, "addicted" refers to one who seeks, searches for, and pursues sensual pleasures; one whose conduct is such, who is abundant in it, who values it highly, who is inclined toward it, who tends toward it, who leans toward it, who is devoted to it, and who is dominated by it—such a person is "addicted to sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, one who, through the influence of craving, seeks out forms (rūpa) is also so addicted.
In sounds … [and so on] … in odors … in tastes …

He seeks tangibles; he is characterized by them, abounds in them, makes them heavy, is inclined toward them, tends toward them, leans toward them, is intent upon them, and has them as his dominant concern—he too is devoted to sensual pleasures.
And whoever, through the influence of craving, acquires forms, sounds... [and so on].
If one acquires odors...
tastes...

tactile objects, being inclined toward them, frequenting them, cherishing them, leaning toward them, tending toward them, flowing toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them—that person too is devoted to sensual pleasures.
Whoever enjoys forms through craving,
sounds … [and so on] … smells … [and so on] …

If one enjoys tastes... or tangibles, being characterized by them, abounding in them, regarding them as heavy, inclined toward them, leaning toward them, tending toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them, then he too is devoted to sensual pleasures.

Just as a quarreler is devoted to quarreling, a laborer is devoted to labor, one wandering for alms is devoted to his range, and a meditator is devoted to meditation; so too is such a person devoted to sensual pleasures.

In the same way, whoever seeks, searches for, and pursues sensual pleasures—practicing them, being full of them, making them weighty, inclining toward them, leaning toward them, tending toward them, being intent upon them, and having them as his dominant concern—is one who is devoted to sensual pleasures.
Whoever, through the influence of craving, seeks out forms...
[and so on] ...whoever, through the influence of craving, acquires forms... [and so on].
And whoever enjoys forms through craving, [or] sounds … pe … smells … [or] tastes … [or] tangibles … [or] mental phenomena through craving, [is likewise bound].

When one enjoys tastes... or tangibles, being habituated to them, abounding in them, cherishing them, inclined toward them, leaning toward them, tending toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them—that person is also addicted to sensual pleasures.
Thus it is called "heedless."
Heedlessness should be described as the relinquishing or the non-renewal of the mind toward bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct; or toward the five strands of sensual pleasure;

or as the lack of earnestness, the lack of constancy, the lack of steadfastness, the sluggish state, the abandonment of desire, and the abandonment of the burden in the cultivation of wholesome states.
Non-cultivation, non-development, non-repetition, lack of resolve, and lack of application; such negligence, neglecting, and state of being negligent—this is called negligence (*pamāda*).
One should not personally cultivate what is indulged in by the negligent, nor should one personally cultivate what is neglected by oneself.
"One should not associate with, should not cultivate, should not frequent, should not dwell upon, should not practice, should not engage in,
and should not conduct oneself by undertaking [such things]"— thus,
one should not associate with those who are addicted and negligent; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore that Paccekabuddha said:
“One should avoid a wicked companion,
one who sees no harm and is intent on what is crooked.”
One should not associate with one who is addicted to sensual pleasures or who is negligent;
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One should cultivate friendship with one who is learned and a bearer of the Dhamma.
Having understood the meanings and dispelled doubt, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros— having found a noble and eloquent friend.
"One should associate with one who is learned and a bearer of the Dhamma": he is a friend who is learned, a retainer of what has been heard, an accumulator of what has been heard.

Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the entirely complete and pure holy life—such teachings as these are well-learned and retained by him.
They are well-mastered by speech, examined by the mind, and thoroughly penetrated by view.
"Upholders of the Dhamma" means those who uphold the Dhamma:

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), legends (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical treatises (vedalla).

"One should associate with one who is learned and a bearer of the Dhamma" means: one should associate with, cultivate, serve, attend upon, frequent, and follow as a companion one who is both learned and a bearer of the Dhamma.
"A friend who is sublime and eloquent" means: such a friend is sublime in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"Endowed with ready wit": there are three kinds of those endowed with ready wit—the one endowed with ready wit regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti*), the one endowed with ready wit regarding inquiry (*paripucchā*), and the one endowed with ready wit regarding realization (*adhigama*).
What is the one endowed with ready wit regarding the scriptures?

In this case, someone has mastered the word of the Buddha—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical teachings.
Relying on that mastery, he becomes inspired:
this is one who possesses inspired eloquence through mastery.
What is one who possesses ready wit through inquiry?
Here, someone is able to inquire about the meaning, the method, the characteristic, the reason, and the possible and impossible.
Relying on such inquiry, he becomes possessed of ready wit.
This one possesses the eloquence of inquiry.
Who possesses the eloquence of realization?
Here, someone has realized the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases for spiritual power.
The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four noble paths,
the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical knowledges, and the six direct knowledges:
their meaning is known, the Dhamma is known, and the language is known.
When the meaning is known, the meaning becomes manifest; when the Dhamma is known, the Dhamma becomes manifest; when the language is known, the language becomes manifest.
Knowledge regarding these three is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
That Paccekabuddha was endowed with, fully endowed with, arrived at, fully arrived at, possessed of, fully possessed of, and equipped with this analytical knowledge of perspicuity.
Therefore, the Paccekasambuddha is eloquent.
For one who has no mastery of the scriptures, no thorough inquiry, and no realization—what would he have to express?
Thus, [he seeks] a sublime friend who is eloquent.

Having understood the meanings, they have removed their doubt— having understood their own welfare, having understood the welfare of others, having understood the welfare of both, having understood the welfare pertaining to the present life,
having understood the welfare pertaining to future lives, and having understood the ultimate goal; having directly known,
known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest, they have removed, overcome, and abandoned doubt.
"One should dispel it, bring it to an end, and lead it to non-existence"—
having understood the meanings and removed doubt, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus spoke that Paccekasambuddha.
“One should associate with one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma,
a noble friend who is eloquent;
having understood the meanings and dispelled doubt, [one should practice].”
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros’s horn.
Without adorning oneself with worldly play, delight, or sensual pleasure,
and without looking back at them;
Abstaining from places of dissipation, speaking the truth,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros,
looking upon worldly play, delight, and sensual pleasure with indifference.
Play is of two kinds:
bodily play and verbal play ... [as follows] ...
this is bodily play ... [as follows].
This is verbal sport.
"Rati" is a designation for non-discontent; such is the meaning of "rati."
"‘Sensual pleasure’ was said by the Blessed One; for it has been said:
‘Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.
What five?’”
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … [and so on].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
“Monks, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure.
‘In the world’ means in the human world—
in the world’s play, delight, and sensual pleasure.”

"Without adorning, without looking back" means: having not adorned, having become indifferent toward, having abandoned, having dispelled, having brought to an end, and having caused the disappearance of play, delight, and sensual pleasure in the world—he is "without adorning, without looking back.
He is "abstaining from the basis for adornment, a speaker of truth."
Adornment: there are two kinds of adornment—there is the adornment of the householder and there is the adornment of the homeless one.
What is the adornment of the householder?
Hair and beard, garlands, perfumes, ointments, ornaments, jewelry, clothing, outer garments, and turbans;
anointing, rubbing, bathing, and massaging; mirrors, collyrium, garlands, perfumes, and ointments;
face powder, face paste, hand-bands, topknot-bands, staffs, flutes, swords, and parasols.
A variegated sandal, a turban, a jewel, a yak-tail fan, or white garments with long borders—
this is the ornamentation of a householder. What is the ornamentation of one who is not a householder?

Adornment with robes, adornment with alms-bowls, adornment with lodgings, or the adornment, decoration, playing, sporting, greed, state of greed, fickleness, and restlessness regarding this putrid body or external requisites—this is the adornment of the householder.
"A speaker of truth": that Paccekasambuddha was a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, reliable, trustworthy, and non-deceptive.
One who stays aloof from, abstains from, desists from, has emerged from, is detached from, is liberated from, and is disjoined from the world’s grounds for adornment,
and dwells with a mind free from boundaries—
such a one, abstaining from the grounds for adornment, speaking the truth, should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Therefore that Paccekabuddha said:
“Having not adorned nor looked back upon play, delight, and sensual pleasure in the world;”
Abstaining from the grounds for adornment, speaking the truth,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Son, wife, father, and mother—
Having abandoned wealth, grain, and kinsmen,
as well as all sensual pleasures according to their extent,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Son, wife, father, and mother.
Regarding "sons," there are four kinds of sons:
the son born of one's own body (*atraja*), the son born of the field (*khettaja*), the son given (*dinnaka*), and the pupil (*antevāsika*).
"Wives" (dārā) means wives.
"Father" means he who is the progenitor.
"Mother" means she who is the progenitress.
One's son, wife, father, and mother;

and wealth and grain, as well as kinsmen—these are what are called "wealth. By "wealth" is meant gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, refined gold, ruby, and cat's-eye.
By "grain" is meant the crops of the preceding and following harvests.
"Grain of the preceding season" (pubbaṇṇa) refers to rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and rye.
"Grain of the following season" (aparaṇṇa) refers to vegetables for soup.
"Relatives" (bandhavā) means four kinds of relatives: [mother, father, brother, and sister].
Kinsmen by birth are relatives; kinsmen by clan are relatives; kinsmen by friendship are relatives;
kinsmen by craft are relatives—wealth and grain are also relatives.
Having abandoned sensual pleasures according to their measure...
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures:
sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
these are called sensual pleasures as objects... [etc.]...
These are called the defilement-desires (*kilesakāmā*).
"Having abandoned desires" means having fully understood object-desires (*vatthukāma*), and having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the defilement-desires.

"Having abandoned desires according to their nature" means that those defilements which were abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) are not repeated, not returned to, and not revisited.
Those defilements abandoned by the path of once-returning …pe… those defilements abandoned by the path of non-returning … those defilements abandoned by the path of arahantship— one does not repeat,
does not return to, and does not go back to those defilements. Thus it is called "non-returning."
Having abandoned sensual pleasures as they arise, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore that Paccekasambuddha said:
“Son and wife, father and mother...”
Having abandoned wealth, grain, and kinsmen,
as well as sensual pleasures beyond measure,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This is a bondage; here there is only limited happiness, little gratification, and much suffering.
Knowing this to be a snare, the wise person—
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

"Attachment" (saṅga) here means that which is limited, a source of pleasure, or rather, attachment, or a fishhook, or bait, or a snag, or an impediment; this is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Regarding "limited and a source of pleasure here," it was said by the Blessed One: [as follows].
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure.
What five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust... [and so on for the other sense objects].”
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Whatever happiness and joy arise in dependence upon these five strands of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure.
"This happiness is meager, this happiness is trifling, this happiness is slight, this happiness is inferior, this happiness is base,
this happiness is a mere trifle"— this is a bond,

for here the pleasure is limited. "Little is the gratification, suffering is more abundant here"— thus have sensual pleasures been described by the Blessed One as having little gratification, much suffering, and much despair.
The danger here is even greater.

The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton; the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat; the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a grass torch;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing embers; the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a dream.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods; the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like the fruits of a tree;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a sword and a slaughterhouse; the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like spears and stakes;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like the head of a serpent—bringing much suffering and much despair, for herein the danger is greater.
Little gratification is there, but suffering is more abundant.

Knowing that "this is a snare"—whether one calls it a snare, or a hook, or bait, or a place where one gets stuck, or a bond, or an impediment—this is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure. As for the word "iti":
it is a junction of words, a connection of words, a completion of words, a combination of syllables, a smoothness of phonemes, and a sequence of words; this is what "iti" means.
One who possesses intelligence, one who is wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
Having understood that this is a hook (*gaḷa*), one who possesses intelligence understands it as a hook;

having understood it as a baited line, having understood it as bait, having understood it as a snag, having understood it as a bond, and having understood it as an impediment—one who has thus known, weighed, scrutinized, discerned, and made manifest [the danger].
Knowing that this is a fetter, the wise one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:
"This is a bond; here, happiness is but meager."
Little is the gratification here, but suffering is greater;
knowing this to be a mere snare,
the wise one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having torn asunder the fetters,
like a water-dweller breaking through a net in the water,
he does not turn back, like a fire that has consumed its fuel.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having torn asunder the fetters refers to the ten fetters:

the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, [the fetter of attachment to existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of miserliness, the fetter of ignorance, and the fetter of agitation].
The fetter of clinging to rules and observances, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, and the fetter of ignorance. “Having torn apart the fetters” means:
having torn apart, having completely torn apart, having abandoned, having dispelled, having brought to an end, and having reduced to non-existence—the ten fetters;
thus, “having torn apart the fetters.”
"Like a water-dweller breaking through a net": "net" refers to a web of thread;
"salila" refers to water;
"water-dweller" refers to a fish.
Just as a fish, having broken through, torn apart, burst, shattered, and completely destroyed a net, moves about, dwells, conducts itself, turns about, protects, preserves, and maintains its life;
even so, there are two nets—the net of craving and the net of views... [as before] ...this is the net of craving... [as before].
This is the net of views.
For that paccekabuddha, the net of craving has been abandoned and the net of views has been relinquished.

Because the net of craving has been abandoned and the net of views has been relinquished, that paccekabuddha does not cling to forms, does not cling to sounds, does not cling to odors ... [and so on] ... [as before].

He does not cling, grasp, become bound, or be obstructed by phenomena seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; he dwells with a mind that has gone out, escaped, is liberated, and is detached, free from the boundaries of the world—like a water-dweller who has broken through a net.
"Like a fire that, having burned its fuel, does not turn back" means just as a fire, while burning its supply of grass and wood, moves forward without turning back.
In the same way, those defilements that have been abandoned by that Paccekasambuddha through the path of stream-entry,
he does not produce them again, does not return to them, and does not go back to them; [the same applies to] through the path of once-returning … pe … through the path of non-returning …
"By means of the path of arahantship, those defilements which have been abandoned are not repeated, not returned to, and not revisited;
like a fire that has burned and does not turn back, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Thus said that Paccekasambuddha.
Having torn asunder the fetters,
like a water-dweller breaking through a net in the water,
he does not turn back, like a fire that has consumed its fuel.
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
With downcast eyes and not fidgeting with the feet,
guarding the sense faculties and protecting the mind.
Unflooded and unburning,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Regarding the phrase "with downcast eyes and not fidgety with the feet," how does one have downcast eyes?
Here, a certain bhikkhu is fickle of eye and possessed of fickleness of eye. Thinking,
"I shall see what has not been seen" and "I shall transcend what has been seen," he is devoted to wandering from monastery to monastery,

from park to park, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city, from kingdom to kingdom, and from country to country, on long journeys and unstable wanderings for the sake of seeing forms.
Thus his eye is cast about. Or else,
when a bhikkhu has entered among the houses and is walking along a street, he goes without restraint,
looking at an elephant, looking at a horse, looking at a chariot, looking at a foot soldier, or looking at boys.
He walks looking at young girls, looking at women, looking at men, looking at the marketplace, looking at the doorways of houses,
looking upward, looking downward, and glancing about in all directions and intermediate points.
In this way too, his vision is distracted.
Alternatively, when a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics;
and because he dwells with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states— might flow in after him,
he does not practice for its restraint, nor does he guard the faculty of the eye.
He does not exercise restraint over the faculty of the eye;
thus he is one whose eye is cast about.
Or again, as some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals given in faith, remain devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these: namely—
Dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical performances, storytelling, hand-clapping, drumming, cymbals, clowns, acrobats, outcasts,
bamboo-pipe players, water-splashing, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights,
goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, stick-fighting, boxing, and wrestling.
Or [he attends] to battles, military parades, the arraying of armies, or the inspection of troops.
Thus he is devoted to such frivolous spectacles.
In this way, too, his vision is distracted.
How does one have downcast eyes?
Here, a certain bhikkhu is not fickle-eyed, nor is he possessed of fickle eyes. He thinks:
"What has not been seen is to be seen; what has been seen is to be transcended. Thus he has downcast eyes.
He was not devoted to long journeys or unsettled wandering for the sake of seeing sights, from monastery to monastery, from park to park, from village to village,
from town to town, from city to city, from kingdom to kingdom, or from province to province.
Thus he has downcast eyes.
Alternatively, when a bhikkhu has entered among the houses and is walking along a street, he goes restrained;
he does not look at an elephant, nor look at a horse, nor look at a chariot, nor look at a foot soldier, nor look at boys.
He walks looking ahead, not looking at young girls, not looking at women, not looking at men, not looking at the marketplace,
not looking at the doorways of houses, not looking upward, not looking downward, and not glancing about in the various directions.
In this way too, he has his eyes cast down.
Or else, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its general appearance nor grasp at its secondary details.
For if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when the eye faculty is unguarded, evil and unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint, guards the eye faculty, and achieves restraint over the eye faculty.
In this way, too, he has downcast eyes.
Or else, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals provided by the faithful, remain devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these: namely—
Dancing, singing, instrumental music... [and so on] ...or watching military parades.
Thus he abstains from such frivolous spectacles.
In this way too, he has downcast eyes.
And how is one "fickle with the feet"?
Here, a certain monk is fickle with his feet, possessed of fickle-footedness:

he is intent on wandering from monastery to monastery, from park to park, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city, from kingdom to kingdom, from province to province, engaged in long journeys and unsettled wandering.
In this way too, he is one who fidgets with his feet.
Alternatively, a bhikkhu is one who fidgets with his feet within the monastery grounds, being possessed of such foot-fidgeting;
for no purpose, for no reason, with an agitated and unpeaceful mind, he goes from one courtyard to another, from one dwelling to another.
He goes from one carriage to another carriage; he goes from one palace to another palace;
he goes from one upper chamber to another upper chamber; he goes from one cave to another cave; he goes from one shelter to another shelter; he goes from one hut to another hut;

he goes from one gabled house to another gabled house; he goes from one watchtower to another watchtower; he goes from one upper story to another upper story; he goes from one turret to another turret.
He goes from the assembly hall to the assembly hall, from one pavilion to another pavilion,
from the foot of one tree to the foot of another tree; or wherever the bhikkhus sit or walk,
there he is the companion of one, or the third of two, or the fourth of three.
Therein, he indulges in much idle chatter, namely:
talk of kings, talk of thieves, [and so forth]...
talk of whether things exist or do not exist.
In this way, too, he is one who fidgets with his feet.

But that Paccekasambuddha, being "not one who fidgets with his feet," is one who has abstained from, desisted from, refrained from, emerged from, escaped from, and is liberated from fidgeting with the feet;
he is dissociated from it and, with a mind for which there are no boundaries [to such conduct], he delights in seclusion and rejoices in seclusion.
Devoted to internal mental tranquility, not neglecting meditative absorption, endowed with insight, one who cultivates solitude,
a meditator delighting in jhāna, devoted to unity, and regarding his own welfare as paramount—
he casts down his eyes and does not fidget with his feet.
"With guarded sense faculties and a protected mind. Regarding "guarded sense faculties":
that Paccekasambuddha, upon seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has seen a form with the eye, there should arise in him covetousness or dejection, unwholesome states that would overwhelm the mind, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye-faculty and attains restraint over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one dwells with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states— might flow in,
one practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of mind, and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
Guarded in the sense-faculties.
"With the mind’s door guarded" means with the mind’s door protected—
thus he is "guarded in the sense-faculties, with the mind’s door guarded."
“Uninhibited and burning”—for this was said by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Friends, I will teach you the discourse on the uninhibited and the discourse on the inhibited.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
“And how, friends, is one ‘tainted’?”

"Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu becomes intent upon a pleasing form and becomes repelled by a displeasing form; he dwells with unmindfulness of the body and with a limited mind.
He does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on]."

Having cognized a phenomenon with the mind, he becomes attached to phenomena that are pleasing and feels aversion toward phenomena that are unpleasing; he dwells without mindfulness established in the body and with a limited mind.
He does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome phenomena cease without remainder.
This, friends, is called a monk who is "outflowing" regarding forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on].
He is corrupted by mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.
And, friends, if Māra approaches such a bhikkhu dwelling in this way, even from the eye, Māra will surely find an opening; Māra will find an objective basis.
If he approaches him from the ear... [and so on].
If Māra approaches him even from the mind, Māra will surely find an opening; Māra will surely find a foothold.
It is just as if, friends, there were a hut of reeds or a hut of grass, dry and parched for three years.
If a man were to approach it from the eastern direction with a burning grass torch, the fire would surely find an opening; the fire would surely find a foothold.
If it were from the western direction...
[and so on] ...if it were from the northern direction...
[and so on] ...if it were from the southern direction...
Even if a man were to approach it from the direction below, or from the direction above,
or from any direction whatsoever with a blazing grass torch, the fire would certainly find an opening and the fire would find a foothold.
In the same way, friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu who dwells thus, even through the eye, Māra will surely find an opening; Māra will surely find an objective basis.
If Māra approaches him through the ear … [and so on] … or if Māra approaches him through the mind, Māra will surely find an opening; Māra will surely find an objective basis.
"Friends, when a bhikkhu dwells in such a way, forms overcome him, he does not overcome forms;
sounds overcome the bhikkhu, he does not overcome sounds;
odors overcome the bhikkhu, he does not overcome odors."
Flavors overwhelmed the bhikkhu; the bhikkhu did not overwhelm flavors.
Tangibles overwhelmed the bhikkhu; the bhikkhu did not overwhelm tangibles.
Mental phenomena overwhelmed the bhikkhu; the bhikkhu did not overwhelm mental phenomena.
This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who has overcome forms, overcome sounds, overcome odors, overcome tastes, overcome tactile objects,
and overcome mental phenomena; one who has overcome, not being overcome, and whom evil,
unwholesome states— defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death— have overcome.
In this way, friends, one is defiled.
And how, friends, is one undefiled?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not become fixated on a pleasing form, nor does he feel aversion toward a displeasing form; he dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind of immeasurable scope.
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Having heard a sound with the ear...

[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not intent upon agreeable phenomena and does not feel aversion toward disagreeable phenomena; he dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind of immeasurable scope.
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who is untainted regarding forms cognizable by the eye...
[and so on] ...untainted regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.
"Friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu who dwells in such a way, even through the eye, Māra will find no opening and will find no foothold;
if Māra approaches him even through the ear... [and so on] ...even through the mind, Māra will find no opening and will find no foothold."
"Friend, it is just as if there were a gabled house or a gabled hall with thick clay walls and a smooth plaster coating.
Even if a man were to approach from the eastern direction with a blazing grass torch, the fire would find no way in,
nor would the fire find an opening."
If it were from the western direction...
if it were from the northern direction...
if it were from the southern direction...
Even if a man were to approach it from the direction below, or from the direction above,
or from any direction whatsoever with a blazing grass torch, the fire would find no way in and the fire would find no foothold.
In the same way, friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu who dwells thus from the eye, Māra will find no opening and will find no foothold;
if Māra approaches him from the ear … [and so on] … if Māra approaches him from the mind, Māra will find no opening and will find no foothold.
Living in such a way, friends, a bhikkhu overcomes forms; forms do not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcomes sounds; sounds do not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcomes odors; odors do not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu has overcome tastes; tastes have not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu has overcome tangibles; tangibles have not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu has overcome mental phenomena; mental phenomena have not overcome the bhikkhu.

"Friends, this monk is called one who has overcome form, overcome sound, overcome odor, overcome taste, overcome tangible objects, and overcome mental phenomena; he is the overcomer, not the one overcome.
He has overcome those evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth, aging, and death.
It is in this way, friends, that one is unsullied."
Unflooded.
"Not burning" means not burning with the fever born of lust, not burning with the fever born of hatred, and not burning with the fever born of delusion—
thus, unflooded and unburning, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Therefore that Paccekasambuddha said:
"With downcast eyes and not fidgety with his feet,
with sense-faculties guarded and mind protected;”
“Unflooded, unburning,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the marks of a householder,
Like the Pārichattaka tree with its dense foliage,
one who has gone forth clad in saffron robes should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Having removed the marks of a householder": the "marks of a householder" are said to be the hair of the head and the beard...
up to ... or long-fringed garments.
"Having removed the marks of a householder" means having shaved off the marks of a householder, having completely shaved them off, having set them aside, having laid them down.
Having cast off the marks of a householder:

"Like the Pārichattaka tree with its foliage fully spread"—just as that Pārichattaka *koviḷāra* tree has thick leaves and foliage and provides abundant shade, even so that Paccekasambuddha wears his bowl and robes complete—thus:
"Like the Pārichattaka tree with its foliage fully spread."
"Clad in saffron robes, having gone forth" means that the Paccekabuddha, having severed all the impediments of the household life,
having severed the impediment of wife and children, having severed the impediment of relatives, having severed the impediment of friends and companions,
and having severed the impediment of hoarding, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and departed from the home.

Having gone forth into homelessness and attained the state of possessing nothing, he wanders alone, dwells alone, moves alone, conducts himself alone, protects himself, maintains himself, and sustains himself—one who has gone out clad in saffron robes; thus:
"One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros."
Therefore that Paccekabuddha said:
“Having cast off the marks of a householder,
like the Pārichattaka tree with its dense foliage;”
“Clad in saffron robes, having gone forth,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The third chapter.
4. Fourth Chapter:
Not being greedy for flavors, not being fickle, not supporting others, and wandering from house to house in regular succession.
With a mind unattached to any family,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros;
not being greedy for flavors, one is free from longing.
