Taste is of these kinds: the taste of roots, the taste of stalks, the taste of bark, the taste of leaves, the taste of flowers, and the taste of fruits; sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, astringent, mild, unpleasant, cold, and hot.
There are some recluses and brahmins who are greedy for tastes;
seeking the finest flavors with the tip of their tongues, they wander about.
Having obtained something sour, they seek what is not sour; having obtained what is not sour, they seek what is sour.
Having obtained something sweet, they seek what is not sweet; having obtained what is not sweet, they seek what is sweet.
Having obtained something bitter, they seek what is not bitter; having obtained what is not bitter, they seek what is bitter.
Having obtained something pungent, they seek what is not pungent; having obtained what is not pungent, they seek what is pungent.
Having obtained something salty, they seek what is not salty; having obtained what is not salty, they seek what is salty.
Having obtained something alkaline, they seek what is not alkaline; having obtained what is not alkaline, they seek what is alkaline.
Having obtained something bitter, they seek what is not bitter; having obtained what is not bitter, they seek what is bitter.
Having obtained something pungent, they seek what is not pungent; having obtained what is not pungent, they seek what is pungent.
Having obtained something sweet, they seek what is not sweet; having obtained what is not sweet, they seek what is sweet.
Having obtained cold, they seek heat; having obtained heat, they seek cold.
Whatever they obtain, they are not satisfied with it, but seek something else after another.
They are attached, greedy, infatuated, obsessed, clinging, stuck, and bound to pleasant tastes.
That craving for taste has been abandoned by that paccekabuddha, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and incapable of arising again in the future.
Therefore, that paccekabuddha consumes food with wise reflection:
"Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment."
"Only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
that is to say: 'I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and I shall have sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
Just as one might apply ointment to a wound only for the sake of healing it, or just as one might oil a cart-axle only for the sake of its movement...
For the sake of carrying the burden, just as one might consume the flesh of one’s own son as food solely for the sake of crossing a wilderness,
even so that Paccekasambuddha, reflecting thoroughly,
consumes food: "Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment."
"Only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
thus, I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and I shall have sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
Thus, being detached, secluded, withdrawn, emerged, escaped, and liberated from craving for tastes, he dwells with a mind that is free from boundaries.
Not being greedy for tastes.
"Lolupa" refers to greed; it is craving.
That which is lust, infatuation... [as before] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
That greed and craving have been abandoned by that paccekabuddha, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the paccekabuddha is "not greedy"—
he is not greedy because he does not harbor attachment to flavors.
"Supporting no others, wandering for alms from house to house":
regarding "supporting no others," that Paccekasambuddha supports only himself and not others.
This is what is meant by "supporting no others."
Tamed, established in the essence,
with taints exhausted and faults vomited out—
him I call a brahmin.
"Not supporting others" and "wandering for alms in regular succession": that Paccekasambuddha, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe,
enters a village or town for alms with body guarded,
speech guarded, mind guarded, with mindfulness established, and sense faculties restrained.
"With downcast eyes, perfected in deportment, and not bypassing families, he wanders for alms"—this refers to one who does not support others and who goes on an uninterrupted round.
"With a mind unattached from family to family": there are two reasons by which the mind becomes attached.
One whose mind is bound is either one who places oneself low and places another high, or one who places oneself high and places another low.
How does one place oneself low and place another high with a bound mind? [Thinking:
"You have been very helpful to me; it is by depending on you that I obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
“Whatever others think I should give or do, they do so out of regard for you and because they see you.
Even my ancient maternal and paternal name and clan have disappeared; I am now known by you simply as ‘the follower of such-and-such a family, the follower of such-and-such a family.’”
Thus, by placing oneself low and placing another high, one is bound by attachment.
How is it that by placing oneself high and placing another low, one is bound by attachment?
"I have been of great benefit to you; it is because of me that you have gone for refuge to the Buddha and for refuge to the Dhamma."

She has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; she abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
To you I give the recitation, I give the opportunity for questioning, I explain the Uposatha, and I authorize the building work.
"And yet you, having abandoned me, honor, revere, esteem, and worship others.
Thus, by exalting himself and degrading another, he becomes one whose mind is bound.
"With a mind unattached to family" means that the Paccekasambuddha has a mind free from the hindrance of attachment to families.
He is one whose mind is unattached to the impediment of a group; his mind is unattached to the impediment of a dwelling;
his mind is unattached to the impediment of robes; his mind is unattached to the impediment of almsfood;
his mind is unattached to the impediment of lodgings; [his mind is unattached] to the impediment of medicinal requisites for the sick.
"He is one whose mind is unattached" means:
he is one whose mind is unattached to family after family; let him wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus spoke that Paccekasambuddha.
“Not being greedy for flavors, free from longing,
not supporting others, wandering for alms from house to house with a mind unattached to family after family.”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind,
having dispelled all secondary defilements;
"Unreliant, having severed the fault of attachment, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind—having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), and the hindrance of ill will (*byāpāda-nīvaraṇa*)... [and so forth].

Having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent the hindrance of sloth and torpor … the hindrance of restlessness and remorse … the hindrance of doubt, and having become quite secluded, [he dwells].
"Secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion"—
this is "having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind."

"Having dispelled all defilements": lust is a defilement of the mind, hatred is a defilement of the mind, delusion is a defilement of the mind; anger... resentment... [and so on] ...all unwholesome volitional formations are defilements of the mind.

"Having dispelled all defilements" means: having dispelled, driven out, abandoned, removed, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent all the defilements of the mind—this is "having dispelled all defilements."
"Independent, having severed the fault of attachment.
"Independent" refers to two kinds of dependence:
dependence on craving and dependence on views... [and so forth].
This is the dependence on craving... [and so forth] ...this is the dependence on views.
Affection: there are two kinds of affection.
There is the affection of craving and the affection of views...
[as before] ...this is the affection of craving... [as before] ...this is the affection of views.
"Hatred" means: that which is the mind's irritation, resentment, hostility, opposition, anger, provocation, intense provocation; hatred, malice, intense malice;
the corruption of the mind, mental corruption, wrath, being wrathful, state of being wrathful;
hatred, hating, state of hating; corruption, becoming corrupt, state of being corrupt; ferocity, abruptness, displeasure of the mind.
"Independent, having severed the fault of attachment"— this means that the Paccekasambuddha, having cut, severed, utterly eradicated,

abandoned, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent both the attachment of craving (*taṇhāsneha*) and the attachment of views (*diṭṭhisneha*), as well as hatred (*dosa*), is independent of the eye,
independent of the ear... [and so on].

"Unreliant, unattached, not approaching, not clinging, not obsessed, having gone forth, escaped, liberated, and dissociated from things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—he dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries. Thus:
"Unreliant, having cut off the fault of affection, let one wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This is what that Paccekasambuddha said.
“Having abandoned the five hindrances that cloud the mind,
having dispelled all secondary defilements,
being independent and having severed the fault of attachment— ”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having turned one’s back on both pleasure and pain,
as well as prior joy and grief;
Having attained equanimity and pure serenity,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having turned one's back on both pleasure and pain, as well as prior joy and grief— he is a Paccekasambuddha.
"With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity"—
having turned one's back on both pleasure and pain, and on joy and grief beforehand.
"Having attained equanimity and purity of serenity.

Here, "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers to that equanimity, the state of looking on, the state of looking on closely, the evenness of mind, the tranquility of mind, the neutrality of mind, which occurs in the fourth jhāna.

"Serenity" (*samatha*) refers to the mind’s stability, steadfastness, firmness, non-distraction, non-agitation, the state of having an undistracted mind, serenity, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration.

In the fourth jhāna, equanimity and serenity are pure, utterly purified, bright, stainless, free from blemish, devoid of secondary defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability.

"Having obtained equanimity and purified serenity" means: having obtained, gained, found, and acquired both equanimity and serenity in the fourth jhāna—one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Therefore that Paccekabuddha said:
“Having turned one’s back on pleasure and pain,
and likewise on prior joy and grief;”
Having attained equanimity and purified serenity,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros—
one who has initiated energy for the attainment of the supreme goal.
With a mind undaunted and conduct untiring,
firm in exertion and endowed with strength and power,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Exerting energy for the attainment of the ultimate goal": the ultimate goal is called the deathless Nibbāna.

That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—for the sake of attaining, gaining, acquiring, reaching, touching, and realizing that ultimate goal, one exerts energy.
He dwells for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the fulfillment of wholesome states, steadfast, firm in effort,
not relinquishing the burden regarding wholesome states—
thus he is one who has aroused energy for the attainment of the ultimate goal.

"Of unshaken mind and unwearied conduct": that Paccekasambuddha generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; ... [and so on] ...
for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.

“He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... [and so on] ...for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states”—
thus he is one whose mind is not dejected and whose conduct is not indolent.
Or else, he exerts his mind and strives, thinking: "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain;

let the flesh and blood dry up in the body, but as long as I have not attained that which can be attained by human strength, human power, human energy, and human perseverance, my vigor shall not falter."
Thus, with an undaunted mind and unwearied conduct:
"I shall neither eat nor drink;
I shall not go out from the monastery."
"I shall not cast down my gaze as long as the arrow of craving has not been pulled out"—
thus he exerts and strives his mind.
In this way too, one is undaunted in mind and untiring in conduct.
One exerts the mind and strives, thinking: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
In this way too, one is undaunted in mind and untiring in conduct.
“I will not rise from this seat until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging”—thus he exerts and strives with a mind that is not cowed and a conduct that is not indolent.
“I will not descend from this walking path... [and so on].
I shall go out from the monastery;
I shall go out from the half-roofed pavilion;
I shall go out from the palace.
I shall emerge from the hut… I shall emerge from the cave… I shall emerge from the shelter…
"I will go out from the hut...
I will go out from the gabled house...
I will go out from the watchtower..."
"I will go out from the upper story...
I will go out from the high platform...
I will go out from the assembly hall..."
"I will emerge from the pavilion...
I will emerge from the foot of the tree until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging"—thus he exerts and strives his mind.
In this way, too, one is of unshaken mind and untiring conduct.
“On this very forenoon, I will bring forth the noble Dhamma, collect it, attain it, touch it, and realize it”—thus he exerts his mind and strives.
In this way, too, he is one whose mind is not cowed and whose conduct is not indolent. “On this very midday... [and so on]...”
In the evening time … [and so on] … before the meal … after the meal …
the first watch...
the middle watch...
the last watch...
In darkness … in light … in rain …
In winter … in summer … in the first stage of life …

He exerts his mind and strives, thinking: “In the middle stage of life... in the final stage of life, I will bring forth the noble Dhamma, I will gather it, I will attain it, I will touch it, and I will realize it.
In this way, he is one whose mind is not cowed and whose conduct is not indolent.
"Daḷhanikkamo thāmabalūpapanno": that Paccekasambuddha was firm in his undertaking;

he was steadfast in his commitment to wholesome states—namely, good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, good conduct of mind, generosity and sharing, the undertaking of virtue, the observance of the Uposatha, filiality toward mother and father, respect for ascetics and Brahmins, and honoring those who are elders in the family.
"Regarding various other superior wholesome states"—

this refers to firm exertion. "Endowed with steadfastness and strength"— that Paccekasambuddha is possessed of, fully endowed with, has attained, fully attained, is furnished with, and is completely equipped with steadfastness, strength, energy, perseverance, and wisdom.
Firm in effort, endowed with fortitude and strength, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus said that Paccekasambuddha:
"Exerting energy for the attainment of the supreme goal..."
With a mind undaunted and conduct untiring,
firm in effort and endowed with strength and power,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Not neglecting seclusion and meditative absorption,
always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma regarding all phenomena,
and thoroughly comprehending the peril in states of existence—
He should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Not neglecting seclusion and meditation, that paccekabuddha delights in seclusion, rejoices in seclusion,
is devoted to internal mental tranquility, does not abandon jhāna, is endowed with insight, and frequents empty dwellings.
"A meditator, delighting in meditation, devoted to solitude, regarding his own welfare as paramount"—this refers to seclusion.
"Not neglecting meditation": that Paccekasambuddha does not neglect meditation for two reasons:

he is intent upon, devoted to, committed to, engaged in, and dedicated to the arising of the first jhāna if it has not yet arisen; or [he is likewise intent] upon the arising of the second jhāna if it has not yet arisen... [and so on].
Or, being engaged, intent, devoted, committed, and fully absorbed in the arising of the third jhāna that has not yet arisen… or in the arising of the fourth jhāna that has not yet arisen—
in this way too, one does not neglect jhāna.
Alternatively, one cultivates, develops, and frequently practices the first jhāna that has arisen; or the second jhāna that has arisen …pe… or the third jhāna that has arisen;
or the fourth jhāna that has arisen—one cultivates, develops, and frequently practices it.
"Thus he does not neglect meditation"—this refers to one who does not neglect the meditation of seclusion.
"Constantly practicing in accordance with the Dhamma among all things": here, "things" (dhammā) refers to the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on]...
The Noble Eightfold Path. What are the secondary practices?

Right practice; practice that is not contrary; practice in accordance with the goal; practice in accordance with the Dhamma and its sequence; fulfilling the precepts; guarding the doors of the sense faculties; moderation in eating; devotion to wakefulness; mindfulness and clear comprehension.
These are called the secondary qualities (*anudhammā*).

"One who constantly practices in accordance with the Dhamma among these things" means: at all times, at fixed times, continuously, uninterruptedly, without interval, in constant succession, like the ripples of water, in an uninterrupted stream, and persistently—before the meal, after the meal, during the first watch, and during the middle watch.
In the last watch of the night, whether it be dark or light, in the rainy season, the winter, or the summer; in the first stage of life, the middle stage of life,
or the final stage of life— he moves, dwells, conducts himself, behaves, guards, maintains, and sustains [himself]—
thus he is one who constantly lives in accordance with the Dhamma among all phenomena.

“Having comprehended the danger in states of existence”: having comprehended the danger in states of existence as “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” and as “all conditioned phenomena are suffering,” and so forth,
and as “all phenomena are non-self,” and so forth.
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation”—having thus comprehended the peril in states of existence—he is one who has comprehended the peril in existences.
Therefore, he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus said that Paccekasambuddha.
“Not neglecting seclusion and meditative absorption,
always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma regarding all phenomena,
and contemplating the peril in states of existence— ”
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Thus, aspiring for the destruction of craving, being diligent,
not dull-witted or mute, learned, and mindful—
One who has understood the Dhamma, who is certain and resolute,
should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros,
striving heedfully for the destruction of craving.
“Craving” means craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena.
“The destruction of craving” means that one who aspires, desires, approves of, longs for, and yearns for the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion;

the destruction of destiny, the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of rebirth-linking, the destruction of existence, the destruction of saṃsāra, and the destruction of the round—is thus described.
Aspiring to the destruction of craving.

“Diligent” means that the Paccekasambuddha was one who acted with care, one who acted with persistence... [and so on] ...“Diligence regarding wholesome states”—thus, “diligent while aspiring to the destruction of craving.”
"Without stammering, learned, and mindful.
"Without stammering" means that the Paccekasambuddha was wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
"Learned" means that the Paccekasambuddha was one who had heard much, retained what he had heard, and accumulated what he had heard.
Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end,
which proclaim the holy life in its entirety, complete and pure— such teachings as these he has heard much of,
retained in mind, mastered by word, examined by the intellect, and well-penetrated through right view.

That Paccekasambuddha Satīmāti is mindful because he is endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects even what was done long ago and spoken long ago—thus he is "not dull-witted, learned, and mindful.
Regarding the phrase "one who has measured the Dhamma, is resolute, and exerts himself": "measured Dhamma" (saṅkhātadhammo) refers to knowledge.
That which is wisdom, understanding... [and so on] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view. One who has measured the Dhamma:

that Paccekasambuddha is one who has measured the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, weighed the Dhamma, scrutinized the Dhamma, clarified the Dhamma, and fully realized the Dhamma—having measured the Dhamma thus: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent"...

[and so on] ...having measured the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, weighed the Dhamma, scrutinized the Dhamma, clarified the Dhamma, and fully realized the Dhamma thus: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease."
Or else, for that Paccekasambuddha, the aggregates are abbreviated, the elements are abbreviated, the sense bases are abbreviated,
the destinies are abbreviated, the rebirths are abbreviated, the linkings-on are abbreviated, the existences are abbreviated,
the cycles of wandering are abbreviated, and the rounds of existence are abbreviated.
Alternatively, that paccekasambuddha stands at the limit of the aggregates, stands at the limit of the elements, stands at the limit of the sense bases,
stands at the limit of destinations, stands at the limit of rebirths, stands at the limit of reconnection, stands at the limit of existence, stands at the limit of saṃsāra,
stands at the limit of the round, stands at the limit of formations, and stands in his final existence.
Established in his final existence, established as one bearing his last body, he is a Paccekasambuddha.
This is his final birth;
this is his last physical aggregation.
The cycle of birth and death;
for him there is no further becoming.
For that reason, the Paccekasambuddha is one who has fully understood all phenomena.
“Fixed” (*niyata*) refers to the four noble paths, which are called “the fixed course” (*niyāma*).
One who is endowed with the four noble paths is “fixed.
Having reached, attained, acquired, touched, realized, and arrived at the fixed course—this is what is meant by “having reached the fixed course.”
"Exertion" (*padhāna*) refers to energy (*vīriya*). It is the arousal of mental energy,
the undertaking, the striving, the endeavor, the effort, the exertion, the perseverance, the steadfastness, the fortitude,
the unflagging striving, the non-abandonment of desire, the non-laying down of the burden, the grasping of the burden, energy, and the faculty of energy.
The power of energy is right effort.
That paccekasambuddha was endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, equipped with, fully equipped with, and furnished with this striving;
therefore, that paccekasambuddha is called "one who strives."
One who has understood the Dhamma, who is steadfast and resolute in effort, should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore, that Paccekasambuddha said:
“Striving for the destruction of craving, being diligent...”
Free from stammering, learned, and mindful;
having fully understood the Dhamma, resolute and striving,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like a lion untroubled by sounds,
like the wind uncaught in a net,
like a lotus unsullied by water—
"One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.

Like a lion among sounds, neither terrified nor agitated"—just as the lion, the king of beasts, is among sounds unafraid, unperturbed, not terrified, not alarmed, not suspicious, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and does not flee; so too is the Paccekasambuddha.
"He dwells unafraid among sounds, undaunted, not terrified, not agitated, not apprehensive, fearless, intrepid, without terror, not fleeing,
having abandoned fear and dread, with his hair standing on end gone;
thus he is 'like a lion, unafraid among sounds.'"
"Like the wind, unattached in a net":
"The wind" refers to easterly winds, westerly winds, northerly winds, southerly winds; winds with dust, winds without dust;
cold winds, hot winds; limited winds, excessive winds; *verambha* winds, wing-winds, and garuḍa winds.
There are fans made of palm leaves and fans for fanning.
"Net" (*jāla*) refers to a web of thread.
Just as the wind does not cling to, seize, bind, or obstruct a net, even so are there two kinds of nets:
The net of craving and the net of views … [as above] … this is the net of craving … [as above] … this is the net of views.
For that Paccekasambuddha, the net of craving has been abandoned and the net of views has been relinquished.

Because the net of craving has been abandoned and the net of views has been relinquished, that Paccekasambuddha does not cling to forms, does not cling to sounds … [and so on] … he does not cling to, grasp at, become bound by, or be obstructed by phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. He dwells having gone forth, having escaped, being utterly liberated, detached, and with a mind free from boundaries.
"Like the wind not clinging to a net;
like a lotus unsmeared by water. Here, "lotus" refers to the lotus flower.
"Water" refers to water.
Just as a lotus flower is not smeared by water, not defiled, not stained, being unsmeared, undefiled, and unstained—even so there are two kinds of smearing:
the smearing of craving and the smearing of views... [as before] ...this is the smearing of craving... [as before].
This is the smear of views.
For that Paccekasambuddha, the smear of craving has been abandoned and the smear of views has been relinquished.

Because the smear of craving has been abandoned and the smear of views has been relinquished, that Paccekasambuddha does not smear himself with form, he does not smear himself with sound … [and so on] … up to … mental phenomena.

Regarding phenomena seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, he is not smeared, not defiled, not stained; unsmeared, undefiled, unstained, gone forth, escaped, liberated, detached, he dwells with a mind for which the boundaries of the world no longer exist—like a lotus unsmeared by water.
Thus one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
That is what that Paccekasambuddha said.
“Like a lion unperturbed by sounds,
like the wind uncaught in a net,
like a lotus unsullied by water— ”
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Just as a powerful lion, having overpowered [his prey],
wanders having subdued the kings of beasts.
Dwell in remote lodgings;
wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Just as a lion, powerful with its fangs, having overpowered, moves about as the king of beasts, so should one dwell.
The one with strong fangs, whose weapon is his fangs, having overcome, having conquered, having overwhelmed, having exhausted,
and having crushed all animals, moves about, dwells, conducts himself, behaves, protects, maintains, sustains, and lives; likewise, the Paccekasambuddha,
powerful in wisdom and having wisdom as his weapon, having overcome, having conquered, and having overwhelmed all breathing beings and persons through wisdom...
Having exhausted [them] and having crushed [them], he moves, dwells, conducts himself, carries on, protects, maintains, and sustains;
thus, like a lion powerful with its fangs, having overpowered by force, the king of beasts moves having overcome the deer.
"One should frequent remote lodgings" means that just as the lion, the king of beasts, moves and dwells after plunging deep into the forest wilderness.
He moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, and sustains [himself]; even a paccekabuddha resorts to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats—
places that are quiet, noiseless, secluded from people, hidden away from men, and suitable for seclusion.
Thus he goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone;

he enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, sits in seclusion alone, and undertakes walking meditation alone; he wanders, dwells, conducts himself, behaves, protects, maintains, and sustains himself alone.
"Frequent secluded lodgings; wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Thus said that Paccekasambuddha:
"Just as a powerful lion, having overcome [his prey]..."
The king moves about having overcome the deer;
one should frequent remote lodgings and wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Cultivating loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and liberation,
as well as sympathetic joy at the proper time,
one remains unopposed by the entire world.
Let him wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Cultivating loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and deliverance, as well as sympathetic joy, he passes his time; such is the Paccekasambuddha.
With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third... [and so on].

... likewise the fourth ... thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will;
with a mind imbued with compassion ... pe ...
"With a mind imbued with sympathetic joy...
[and] with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—he dwells pervading [the world].
Thus, by practicing loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and liberation, as well as sympathetic joy at the proper time."

"Unopposed by the entire world" means that because loving-kindness has been cultivated, those beings in the eastern direction are not disagreeable to him, as are those beings in the western direction...
[and so on] ...those beings in the northern direction...
and those beings in the southern direction.
Those beings in the eastern intermediate direction… those beings in the western intermediate direction… those beings in the northern intermediate direction…
Those beings in the southern intermediate direction … those beings in the nadir … those beings in the zenith …
Those beings in the ten directions are not repulsive because of the cultivation of compassion … because of the cultivation of sympathetic joy …
Because equanimity has been developed, those beings in the eastern direction … [and so on] … those beings in the ten directions become unrepulsive to him.
"Not being obstructed by the whole world" means not being obstructed by the whole world, not being opposed, not being afflicted, and not being impeded.
Unopposed by the entire world, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:
“Loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and liberation...”
Cultivating joy at the proper time,
and not coming into conflict with the entire world,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
and having torn asunder the fetters,
one should live without fear when the span of life has come to its end.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion.
"Lust" refers to that which is lust, intense lust... [as above] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Hatred" is that which is resentment of the mind... pe ...fury, abruptness, and dissatisfaction of the mind.
"Delusion" is ignorance regarding suffering... pe ...the head of ignorance, delusion, the root of unwholesomeness.

Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion: that Paccekasambuddha, having abandoned, having relinquished, having dispelled, having brought to an end, and having rendered non-existent lust, hatred, and delusion.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
and having torn asunder the fetters— namely,
the ten fetters.
The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion … [and so on] … the fetter of ignorance.

"Having torn apart the fetters" means: having torn apart, crushed, completely crushed, abandoned, dispelled, brought to an end, and reduced to non-existence—the ten fetters—thus it is said, "having torn apart the fetters."
"At the end of life, he is without fear": that Paccekasambuddha, at the conclusion of his life, dwells without anxiety, without terror, without agitation, without apprehension;
he is fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and does not flee; having abandoned fear and dread, he dwells with the hair on his body stilled. Thus it is said.
“Unfrightened at the exhaustion of life, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus said that Paccekasambuddha:
“Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion...”
Having torn asunder the fetters,
being fearless at the end of life,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
People resort to and serve others for the sake of some purpose;
friends without a motive are rare these days.
Human beings are impure in their wisdom regarding their own self-interest.
One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.

They associate with and serve for the sake of some purpose: for the sake of their own welfare, for the sake of another’s welfare, for the sake of the welfare of both, for the sake of welfare in the present life, for the sake of welfare in future lives, or for the sake of the ultimate goal.
They associate, they associate closely, they serve, they attend upon, they serve thoroughly, and they serve repeatedly—for these reasons.
They associate with and serve [others] for the sake of some motive;
those who are friends without a motive are rare today. There are two kinds of friends: the householder friend and the homeless friend …pe…
"This one is a friend who remains a householder...
this one is a friend who has gone forth into homelessness.

'Friends without cause are hard to find today'—these two kinds of friends, being without cause, without motive, without reason, and without condition, are hard to find, difficult to obtain, and very rare."
"Friends without cause are rare these days;
people are wise only for their own sake.
By "wise for their own sake," it means they associate with others for their own benefit, for their own purpose, for their own motive, and for their own reason.
They share, serve, attend upon, associate with, practice, follow, honor,
inquire about, and question— it is thus called wisdom regarding one’s own welfare.
"Unclean people": they are unclean people because they are possessed of unclean bodily action; they are unclean people because they are possessed of unclean verbal action;

they are unclean people because they are possessed of unclean mental action; [they are unclean people] because of unclean taking of life... [and so on] ...because of unclean taking of what is not given... [and so on].
...endowed with impure sexual misconduct,
...impure false speech,
...and endowed with impure divisive speech...
... endowed with impure and harsh speech ...
endowed with impure idle chatter ...
endowed with impure covetousness ...
"Defiled people" means those possessed of impure ill will; "defiled people" means those possessed of impure wrong view;
"defiled people" means those possessed of impure volition; "defiled people" means those possessed of impure aspiration;
"defiled people" means those possessed of impure resolve; they are defiled, base, inferior, and lowly.
The four lowly forms of limited wisdom— namely,
the wisdom concerned with one's own welfare— are impure in human beings.
"One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros."
That Paccekasambuddha is "one" (ekoti) by virtue of what is termed his renunciation; he dwells alone...
[he practices] the eight modes of conduct...
[he is] "like the rhinoceros horn" (khaggavisāṇakappo), just as the horn of a rhinoceros is indeed single and without a second... [and so forth].
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus that Paccekasambuddha said:
“They associate and serve for the sake of some purpose;”
Friends without cause are hard to find these days;
people are impure in their wisdom regarding their own welfare.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Ajita, Tissa, and Metteyya.
Puṇṇaka and then Mettagū;
Dhotaka and Upasīva,
and Nanda and then Hemaka.
Todeyya and Kappa,
both of them, and the wise Jatukaṇṇī;
Bhadrāvudha and Udaya—
And the brahmin Posāla,
the wise Mogharāja,
and Piṅgiya the great seer.
This is the exposition of the sixteen Pārāyanas,
which is like the teaching of the Brāhmaṇas.
For they are indeed that many;
and the expositions of the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta*s are likewise the same.
The expositions are to be known as twofold:
complete and well-characterized.
